papers.title: Decision-Tree-Based Approaches to Brain Mapping and Consciousness Research: Neural Interactions, Emergence and Level Assessment
papers.abstract: Mapping consciousness across the brain requires more than locating isolated activations: it requires explaining how distributed, hierarchical networks integrate information and why awareness varies in strength across contexts. Against this backdrop, decision-tree systems offer an interpretable bridge between complex neuroimaging, electrophysiological, behavioral and physiological data and clinically meaningful states. Their conditional branches can expose how regional activity, connectivity, oscillations and network measures combine to distinguish neural configurations, while ensemble extensions improve predictive flexibility. As evidence accumulated, however, the explanatory value of these models became inseparable from broader mechanisms of consciousness. Predictive-brain accounts, recurrent exchange, excitation–inhibition balance and population-level coordination suggest that trees can identify observable conditions associated with emergent awareness but cannot themselves produce or establish its underlying causal dynamics. Their greatest promise therefore lies in grading consciousness probabilistically, including covert capacities that behavior may miss, rather than enforcing binary classifications. Yet tensions persist between readability and mechanistic truth, regional interpretability and distributed physiology and static prediction and changing brain–environment relationships. Model explanations remain target- and context-dependent, while incomplete data, distributional shifts and concept drift limit generalization. Future progress will require temporally sensitive, uncertainty-aware, multimodal and clinically validated frameworks that connect interpretable decision paths to physiological mechanisms, enabling decision-tree systems to support-not replace-neuroscientific inference about the emergence and modulation of conscious states.

papers.title: Beyond mindfulness: how Buddhist meditation transforms consciousness through distinct psychological pathways
papers.abstract: Buddhist meditation, encompassing practices such as Samatha (focused attention), Vipassana (open monitoring), and Metta (loving-kindness), offers unique pathways for transforming consciousness beyond conventional mindfulness. In this article, we review the studies that explore how these distinct meditative techniques systematically cultivate meta-cognitive insight, emotional regulation, and self-inquiry, facilitating profound shifts in awareness and personal growth. Recent neuroscience and psychology studies show that these techniques influence the mind in different ways: they strengthen attentional stability, reshape self-referential thinking, and reorganize emotional patterns. Such modifications are evident in reorganized brain networks (for example, the default-mode network) and in characteristic EEG patterns. While sharing some parallels with Western mindfulness and hypnosis, Buddhist meditation uniquely emphasizes ethical integration and profound introspection. Challenges remain in objectively measuring advanced meditative states, particularly the experience of “no-self” (anattā), due to the reliance on subjective self-report. Future research should incorporate culturally sensitive methodologies, objective behavioral tasks, and interdisciplinary approaches like neurophenomenology to integrate traditional contemplative wisdom with rigorous scientific inquiry.

papers.title: Cultivating Compassion: The ‘Metta Garden’ as a Spiritual Practice for Ecological Healing and Human Well-being
papers.abstract: As the ecological crisis intensifies, with 45% of flowering plants facing extinction, innovative approaches integrating spiritual practice and environmental conservation are urgently needed. This paper examines the 'Metta Garden' concept developed in Sri Lanka, which synthesizes Buddhist principles of lovingkindness (metta) and interdependence (paṭicca samuppāda) with therapeutic horticulture and biodiversity conservation. Drawing on Plant Humanities methodology and Buddhist ecological philosophy, this study explores how contemplative gardening practices can address both environmental degradation and human well-being simultaneously. The Metta Garden approach employs poison-free cultivation methods, mindful gardening practices, and habitat creation for all beings, grounded in the Buddhist understanding of the four elements (water, fire, air, earth) and non-violence (ahimsa). The design incorporates walking meditation paths that engage all five senses while supporting progressive stages of spiritual development. Drawing on documented outcomes from a five-year case study of the Metta Garden, this paper synthesises existing research and practice evidence to examine how butterfly species recovered from 6 to 64, alongside thriving populations of native bees, birds, and soil organisms. Rather than presenting original empirical data, this article provides a critical review of the garden’s documented outcomes within a Plant Humanities and Buddhist ecological framework. The initiative has fostered significant community engagement through shared harvests, composting programs, and educational activities, creating networks of environmental stewardship and social healing. Therapeutic outcomes include enhanced mental health through stress reduction, increased mindfulness, and strengthened community connections. This research contributes to emerging scholarship in Plant Humanities by demonstrating how traditional Buddhist wisdom can inform contemporary conservation strategies. The Metta Garden model offers scalable applications for urban agriculture, climate resilience, and therapeutic horticulture programs globally, suggesting that integrating spiritual practices with ecological restoration creates pathways toward both environmental healing and human flourishing. The findings indicate that addressing the cultural and psychological dimensions of environmental crisis through contemplative practice may be essential for achieving lasting ecological transformation.

papers.title: Comparison of LSTM- and GRU-Type RNN Networks for Attention and Meditation Prediction on Raw EEG Data from Low-Cost Headsets
papers.abstract: This study bridges neuroscience and artificial intelligence by developing advanced models to predict cognitive states—specifically attention and meditation—using raw EEG data collected from low-cost commercial devices such as NeuroSky and Brainlink. Leveraging the temporal capabilities of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent units (GRUs), the study evaluates their effectiveness in predicting future cognitive states. These predictions have applications in real-time brain–computer interface (BCI) systems, enhancing responsiveness and adaptability in dynamic environments like robotic control. The proposed LSTM model demonstrated superior predictive accuracy for meditation states, achieving a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 10.90, while the GRU model excelled in predicting attention states, with an RMSE of 11.79. Both models outperformed the results provided by the proprietary eSense algorithm, reinforcing the potential of raw EEG data in cognitive-state analysis. Notably, inference times were optimized to under 50 milliseconds, making the models suitable for real-time applications. These findings underline the feasibility of using raw EEG signals from affordable devices for robust real-time prediction, offering a significant step forward in applied neuroscience. This research lays the groundwork for further exploration of RNN architectures in BCI applications, enabling safer, more intuitive, and personalized interactions in assistive technologies and beyond.

papers.title: Effects of Meditation and Yoga on Anxiety, Depression and Chronic Inflammation in Patients with Parkinson’s Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Clinical guidelines recommend a holistic approach to Parkinson’s disease (PD) care, yet randomized trials examining mindfulness-based interventions in this context are scarce. This study investigated the effects of two mindfulness practices – meditation and yoga – on biopsychosocial outcomes in PD patients, including anxiety symptoms, depressive symptoms, motor/nonmotor symptoms, health-related quality-of-life (HRQOL), mindfulness, and stress and inflammation biomarkers, compared to usual care. Methods: 159 participants with a clinical diagnosis of idiopathic PD and a Hoehn and Yahr stage of 1, 2, and 3, were randomized into meditation (n = 53), yoga (n = 52), and control (n = 54). Meditation and yoga were delivered in 90-min groups for 8 weeks. Primary outcomes included anxiety symptoms and depressive symptoms. Secondary outcomes included motor and nonmotor symptoms, HRQOL, mindfulness, and serum levels of interleukin-6, cortisol and TNF-alpha. Assessments were done at baseline (T0), 2 months (T1), and 6 months (T2). Linear mixed models were conducted following intention-to-treat principle. Results: Compared to control, both meditation, and yoga groups had significant improvements in anxiety symptoms (meditation: mean difference [MD] = −1.36, 95% CI: −2.46 to−0.26; yoga: MD = −1.61, CI: −2.70 to −0.52), motor symptoms (meditation: MD = −5.35, CI: −8.61 to−2.09; yoga: MD = −6.59, CI: −9.82 to−3.36), HRQOL (meditation: MD = −2.01, CI: −3.41 to−0.62; yoga: MD = −1.45, CI: −2.83 to−0.08), and describing skills (meditation: MD = 0.97, CI: 0.04–1.89; yoga: MD = 0.92, CI: 0.01–1.84) at T1, and significant reductions in serum interleukin-6 levels (meditation: MD = −1.14, CI: −2.18 to−0.10; yoga: MD = −1.11, CI: −2.09 to−0.13) at T2. Only meditation significantly reduced depression (MD = −1.44, CI: −2.57 to−0.30) at T1 and sustained the motor and HRQOL improvements at T2. Conclusion: Meditation and yoga significantly improved anxiety symptoms, chronic inflammation, motor symptoms, mindfulness-describing facet, and HRQOL in PD patients. Meditation provided additional benefits in reducing depressive symptoms and sustaining motor and HRQOL improvements. papers.title: Mindfulness, cognition, and long-term meditators: Toward a science of advanced meditation
papers.abstract: Abstract Mindfulness meditation is a systematic training in equanimity, sensory clarity, and concentration rooted in ancient contemplative traditions. Here, we synthesized cognitive–behavioral outcomes in long-term meditators (LTMs) resulting from diverse, prolonged meditation practices. Preliminary evidence suggests that LTMs exhibit increased cognitive–sensory integration and decoupling of affective processes, demonstrated by enhanced interoceptive awareness, reduced negative affective pain perception, and more rational decision making. Additionally, LTMs may experience more emotional neutrality, malleable self-boundaries, and altered self-awareness. Neuroimaging findings included increased bottom-up activation, particularly within the salience network (interoception, pain, affect), and reduced connectivity between the executive (dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) and salience (dorsal anterior cingulate cortex) networks (reduced pain). The literature also suggests reduced fear and amygdala activation (mitigated negative affect), increased temporoparietal junction activation (pre-reflective experiential processes, empathy), and altered midline default-mode network activation, which was associated with emotional neutrality and non-ordinary states of consciousness. Methodological limitations restricted the interpretation of trait effects, emphasizing the need for a unified framework to systematically investigate advanced meditation’s states, stages, and endpoints using neurophenomenology. In summary, LTMs display a distinct neurophenomenological gestalt of mindfulness, wherein meditative expertise is reflected in enhanced cognitive flexibility and integration, self-regulation, and non-dual awareness—signifying a potentially important form of embodied cognition.

papers.title: Incidence and Predictors of Meditation-Related Unusual Experiences and Adverse Effects in a Representative Sample of Meditators in the United States
papers.abstract: Estimates suggest that meditation use is comparable to mental-health-service access in the United States. Understanding meditation-related adverse effects (AEs) is therefore critical. We aimed to (a) estimate the incidence of meditation-related unusual experiences and AEs using different methods and (b) identify sociodemographic and health-related characteristics predicting their incidence. We conducted a cross-sectional, population-based survey of 886 U.S. adults (approximately representing population age, gender, and race/ethnicity) stratified by lifetime meditation experience and type. Of the participants, 96.6% reported an unusual experience, 58.4% reported an AE (Inventory of Meditation Experiences), 78.3% endorsed one or more items on the Meditation-Related Adverse Effects Scale, 31.4% endorsed experiencing a challenging/difficult/distressing experience, and 9.1% reported functional impairment because of AEs. In a robust multiple regression, psychological distress, psychoticism, unusual beliefs, and meditation-retreat participation were positively associated with unusual experiences and AEs. It is essential that (a) potential meditators are informed about possible experiences, (b) providers consider risk factors, and (c) AEs are routinely and actively monitored.

papers.title: From Yogic Psychology to Educational Practice: A Conceptual Framework Linking Chitta-Vritti-Nirodha, Attention Regulation, and Meaningful Learning
papers.abstract: The possibility that contemplative disciplines can strengthen attention and thereby support learning has attracted interest across educational psychology, cognitive neuroscience and school-based yoga research. Yet the classical formulation yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ addresses an ethical and soteriological project, not a validated theory of academic performance. This critical narrative review examines the conceptual distance and potential connections between Pātañjala yoga psychology, experimentally studied attention regulation and meaningful learning. Relevant philosophical analysis, cognitive and educational theory, intervention trials and research syntheses were evaluated with particular attention to construct correspondence, comparison conditions, developmental context, educational outcomes and ethical implementation. The evidence supports a conditional, rather than direct, link: contemplative exercises may sometimes improve proximal attentional or emotional-regulatory processes, but improved performance on attention tasks does not establish durable understanding, conceptual change or transfer. School-based syntheses report heterogeneous and generally small benefits, with weaker or absent advantages against active controls and inconsistent effects on achievement. The proposed framework therefore distinguishes philosophical orientation, trainable regulatory practices, cognitive mediators, task-specific engagement, pedagogical mechanisms and learning outcomes. It treats curricular quality, learner agency, developmental suitability and sociocultural context as necessary moderators rather than incidental details. Four falsifiable pathways are advanced, while a competing explanation attributes some observed gains to movement, structured pauses, adult attention or expectancy. The review concludes that contemplative attention training is best understood as an optional enabling condition for well-designed learning activities, not as an alternative to explanation, retrieval, feedback, conceptual discussion or equitable teaching. Research should test mechanisms, potential harms and durable transfer through preregistered active-comparator studies using both attentional and curriculum-aligned measures.

papers.title: An early-stage embodied carbon assessment method for the Global South: Sri Lankan case study
papers.abstract:
Quantifying embodied carbon (EC) is essential for mitigating climate change impacts and reducing excessive use of natural and non-renewable materials. Yet, many Global South countries face several challenges such as data limitations, technical capacity gaps and limited use of EC assessment tools, particularly at early design stage where the greatest reduction potential exists. This study therefore aims to develop an accessible early design stage EC assessment model to support more effective EC management.
 
 
 
 This study employs a mono-method quantitative approach using secondary data from 25 office building projects in Sri Lanka. Data for model development were extracted from architectural drawings and bills of quantities (BOQs) to determine material quantities, while EC coefficients were obtained from Inventory of carbon and energy (ICE) v3.0. Model development integrated multiple linear regression (MLR) technique with life cycle assessment (LCA) principle.
 
 
 
 The findings indicate that the developed model provides accurate and reliable EC estimates using a limited set of early design parameters. Gross internal floor area (GIFA) and external wall area (EWA) were found to be the most influential in determining EC estimations.
 
 
 
 The model provides built environment professionals with a practical and time-efficient tool for estimating EC at the early design stage, supporting informed design decisions, wider adoption in data-scarce contexts, and improved carbon management in the Global South.
 
 
 
 This study is distinctive in providing an accessible EC assessment model specifically tailored to the constraints of Global South contexts, where limited data and technical capacity often hinder effective carbon management.

Phytochemical profiling and larvicidal assessment of Tagetes patula Linn and Phlogacanthus thyrsiformis Nees. flower extracts against Culex quinquefasciatus
papers.abstract: Vector-borne diseases are a significant global health concern, with millions of people affected every year. Mosquitoes remain a major carrier of parasites and pathogens that continue to affect humans. Culex quinquefasciatus is a well-known mosquito vector capable of causing a broad range of diseases, including filariasis. Due to the detrimental effects of chemical insecticides, eco-friendly plant-based chemicals have become a better alternative to control measures. The present research work was undertaken to study the efficacy of methanolic extracts of commonly available plants, viz. T. patula L., Phlogacanthus thyrsiformis Nees. and its combined formulation against the larvae of the C. quinquefasciatus at different sub-lethal concentrations, viz., 250 ppm, 500 ppm, 750 ppm, and 1000 ppm. The study was based on the behavioural changes, larval development, and mortality rate by the standard method. Phytochemical screening was performed, followed by GC-MS for bioactive components responsible for insecticidal activity. On exposure to the initial concentrations of the extract, various damages, including hyperactive wriggling movement, delayed hatching, and damaged bodies, were observed in the mosquito larvae. At higher concentrations of exposure, distorted bodies and delayed moulting were observed, which later led to the morbid condition. The mortality rate of the combined formulation applied to mosquito larvae is more compared to the individual extracts of the chosen plants. These findings demonstrate the pesticidal potential of T. patula L. and P. thyrsiformis Nees. extract against the C. quinquefasciatus, following its impact on physiological and morphological behaviour, suggesting the need for further research on control measures against the mosquito.

papers.title: What enables climate-responsive and resource-efficient office buildings in a small island developing state? a stakeholder-weighted readiness gap analysis
papers.abstract: Climate-responsive and resource-efficient office buildings, often described in practice as green office buildings, are increasingly promoted in Small Island Developing States (SIDS). However, there remains limited understanding of how policy, finance, skills, and supply conditions interact to constrain adoption, as the literature largely focuses on barriers and drivers rather than readiness as a systemic condition. This study aims to examine what enables such buildings in Mauritius through a systems-informed, stakeholder-weighted readiness gap analysis. A mixed-methods approach combined 33 survey responses with five expert interviews. Survey respondents were regrouped into four stakeholder clusters such as developer/owner, government/policy, commercial/advisory, and technical delivery. Weighted Likert-scale responses were normalised into four readiness domains: market and finance, technical and supply, policy and institutional, and collaboration and delivery. Interview evidence was coded into causal relationships to produce a qualitative system map and identify reinforcing adoption traps and leverage points. The largest weighted gaps were found in market and finance readiness (0.735), technical and supply readiness (0.666), and policy and institutional readiness (0.652), while collaboration and delivery showed a lower but still material deficit (0.449). By contrast, respondents expressed strong support for feasible implementation priorities, particularly flood resilience (0.860), life-cycle assessment (0.852), daylighting (0.843), rainwater harvesting (0.843), passive cooling and efficient air-conditioning (0.834), and digital technologies (0.831). The findings show that the main challenge is not the absence of technical pathways, but weak enabling conditions. The paper contributes a multi-stakeholder study and a practical readiness-to-action framework for scaling uptake in SIDS office building markets.

Scope of Ayurvedic Management in the Non-Substance Addiction
papers.abstract: Objectives: Addiction disorder is a major issue, rapidly increasing worldwide. There’re limited treatment options in modern science. Hence before the increasing addiction cases become a global burden, preventive measures should be taken. Ayurveda modalities may hold a satisfactory solution for this, to spread awareness and take preventive measures for addiction, and available treatment options in Ayurveda for de-addiction. This study focuses on the Ayurvedic management of non-substance addiction. Hence this conceptual study is planned. Data source: The classical Ayurvedic Texts with their commentaries, other Ayurvedic and Modern texts, journals, articles, relevant websites were referred. Review methods: Addiction is considered as a chronic, relapsing disorder which involves compulsive use of a substance, thing or activity even after harmful consequences. It’s a mental illness as per Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (DSM-5). In Ayurveda also, non-substance addiction can be involved in Manas Vikar, where the subjects and functions of mind are affected. They can be managed by Ayurveda. Results: Ayurvedic treatments like Medhya Rasayana, Nasya, Shirobhyanga, Satvavajay, Mantra Chanting, Ashwasana, Achar Rasayana, Sadvritta palan, Vyayama, Chitta Vritti Nirodha, Dhyana and Naisthiki Chikitsa can be beneficial for de-addiction. Conclusion: Non-substance addictions can be well treated by Ayurveda.

papers.title: Effects of digital stress-management interventions in breast cancer patients 18 months after intervention access.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Digital stress-management tools show promise, but their long-term impact remains unclear. In the Coping After Breast Cancer (CABC) trial, the app-based stress-management program StressProffen, with either cognitive behavioral therapy intervention (CBI) or a mindfulness-based intervention (MBI), showed no advantage over usual care after six months of access. However, benefits may emerge gradually, as users need time not only to become familiar with the content and techniques, but also to internalize, apply and automatize their use in response to real-life stressors. The a priori defined aims of the current study were to examine; 1) whether extended (18 months) access to the digital stress-management interventions CBI and MBI were associated with changes in perceived stress (stress) (primary outcome), measures of health-related quality of life, mindfulness, fatigue, coping, anxiety, depression, and sleep (secondary outcomes), 2) association between app use and changes in stress level and investigate baseline characteristics as moderators of change in stress in the intervention groups, and 3) identify predictors of change in stress among patients with breast cancer. METHODS: Of 430 patients randomized to MBI, CBI, or usual care, 76% (n = 327) completed the 18-month survey. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess between-group differences in primary and secondary outcomes. Moderator analyses were performed to examine whether specific baseline characteristics modified the intervention effects on stress levels. Predictor analysis of change in stress was performed for the total sample. RESULTS: At 18 months, all three groups showed stable trends over time, with no significant difference between either intervention group and controls. A larger stress reduction was observed among younger participants (≤50 years) in both CBI and MBI compared to controls. Higher baseline stress levels predicted significantly larger stress reductions in the total sample, but the moderator analysis showed that the effects were only significant in the CBI group. CONCLUSION: Neither CBI nor MBI showed statistically significant improvements at 18 months compared to controls. The results however suggest that long-term access to stress management interventions may help young women with breast cancer and those with high initial stress to reduce their stress levels. CLINICALTRIALS: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT04480203.

papers.title: The effect of a seven-week online mindfulness intervention on the relationship between menstrual symptoms and mental health - A non-randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Menstrual symptoms are common among physically active women and may affect their well-being and performance. Moreover, symptom frequency has been associated with mental health in previous studies. Although mindfulness-based interventions (MBI) have shown beneficial effects on psychological and physiological health outcomes, their potential role in the relationship between menstrual and mental health remains unclear. Therefore, this study examined whether participation in an MBI was associated with changes in this relationship. METHODS: 39 physically active students were split into an experimental group (EG; n = 14; 22.68 ± 2.23 years) and a control group (CG; n = 25; 22.76 ± 4.88 years), which conducted a baseline and post-intervention measurement, including a psychometric screening. The CG received no intervention during the study and was offered access to the intervention materials afterwards. Assessed constructs included the 21-item version of the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale and the Menstrual Symptom index (MSi). The MBI was developed based on mindfulness-based stress reduction, incorporating the dimensions of acting with awareness, non-judgmental acceptance, and present-moment attention. RESULTS: At baseline in the control group, MSi scores were positively associated with anxiety (B = 0.16; p = .004) and depression (B = 0.14; p = .012). No significant group × time interactions were observed for depression or stress. For anxiety, the group × time interaction was significant at the grand-mean MSi score (B = - 3.30; 95% CI [- 6.50, - 0.11]; p = .043), whereas the three-way interaction was not significant (p = .054). CONCLUSION: The results indicate that menstrual symptom frequency is associated with mental health outcomes in physically active students. Participation in the MBI was associated with changes in anxiety over time. However, the non-significant three-way interaction provided no conclusive evidence of moderation. These preliminary findings suggest potential benefits of MBI for anxiety in menstrual health context. Future studies should investigate programs that explicitly address menstrual-related aspects. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was registered as 'Impact of an online mindfulness intervention on sleep quality in physically active students' in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS) under the identifier DRKS00038462 on 13 November 2025. Retrospectively registered.

papers.title: Emotion Regulation in Universal Adolescent Mental Health Prevention Programs Delivered by Schools: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adolescence is a developmental period marked by rapid biological, cognitive, and social changes that may precede psychological disorders. Emotion regulation (ER) is critical in adolescence as a transdiagnostic factor relevant to mental health disorders. Universal prevention programs can reduce emerging psychological disorders and fit well within school-based social-emotional learning; however, it is unclear how these programs address adolescents' unique needs, including ER development. METHODS: School-based universal mental health programs were systematically reviewed for inclusion of ER skills and strategies. Four databases yielded 43 articles and 34 unique programs, 19 of which included ER strategies. RESULTS: While 48 distinct ER strategies were identified, the most common were cognitive approaches, mindfulness, and problem solving. Programs without ER components focused more on mental health knowledge and stigma than on skills. Programs with ER skills generally provided more comprehensive psychological content. IMPLICATIONS FOR SCHOOL HEALTH POLICY, PRACTICE, AND EQUITY: ER preventive interventions can serve as broad, population-based strategies to promote mental health, filling important gaps in SEL curricula. CONCLUSIONS: ER content may offer unique benefits by targeting a critical transdiagnostic factor underlying adolescent mental health problems, though further research is needed to establish clear effectiveness and cultural appropriateness.

papers.title: Mindful eating versus prayer before meals for psycho-physiological outcomes in middle-aged women: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Meal-time contemplative practices may provide simple complementary self-care strategies for women during midlife. This study compared the short-term effects of mindful eating, prayer before meals, and routine eating on eating-attitudes, anxiety, and physiological indicators. METHODS: In this assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial, 87 community-dwelling women aged 40-64 years were allocated to mindful eating (ME), prayer before meals (PE), or routine eating control (CONT) for 7 days. Completed baseline and day-7 data were available for 86 participants (CONT, n = 29; ME, n = 28; PE, n = 29). Outcomes included the Eating Attitudes Test-26, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory subscale, blood pressure, body weight, and waist circumference. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used to examine time, group, and time × group effects. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics showed no statistically significant between-group differences. Significant time × group interventions were observed for EAT-26 total scores (F(2,83) = 5.694, p =.005), the Dieting subscale (F(2,83) = 5.054, p =.008), and body weight (F(2,83) = 3.544, p =.033). However, EAT-26 total and Dieting scores increased in the ME group; because higher EAT-26 scores indicate greater eating-related concerns, these findings should not be interpreted as improved eating attitudes. The mean body-weight decrease in the ME group was 0.40kg; this secondary finding was considered exploratory. No significant time × group interactions were found for systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, waist circumference, or state anxiety. CONCLUSIONS: This small, short-duration exploratory RCT identified increase in EAT-26 total and Dieting scores in an unfavorable direction, alongside a small short-term change in measured body weight. The findings do not establish improved eating attitudes, differential effects on blood pressure or state anxiety, or weight-management efficacy. Longer, prospectively registered trial with stronger adherence monitoring and standardized measurements are needed to clarify the clinical significance of these observation.

papers.title: Workplace Policy Awareness, Training, and Supervisory Support as Correlates of Generative Artificial Intelligence Use Among Practicing Nurses.
papers.abstract: AIM: To estimate the prevalence and frequency of generative artificial intelligence (AI) use among practicing nurses and to determine whether four workplace governance conditions were independently associated with use. DESIGN: US-wide nonprobability cross-sectional survey. METHODS: Licensed, practicing nurses in the United States (N = 1136) recruited through a commercial, US-wide nonprobability online panel completed a self-administered questionnaire. Any work-related use in the previous 12 months was modelled using binary logistic regression, and the frequency of clinical use, measured with an unbounded habitual-use item, was modelled using proportional-odds ordinal regression. Both models included workplace policy awareness, training status (training receipt and interest among untrained respondents), supervisor support, and organizational support and adjusted for role, setting, education, experience, age, gender, and geographic region. Sensitivity analyses examined ordinal-covariate coding, the proportional-odds assumption, and support-item specification. RESULTS: In the previous 12 months, 742 nurses (65.3%) reported using a generative AI tool for a work-related task, and 528 (46.5%) reported at least weekly use for clinical tasks on a separate habitual-frequency item without a bounded recall period. The two estimates are not nested because the frequency item used a different reference frame. Each point of supervisor support was associated with higher odds of any use (aOR = 1.42, 95% CI [1.17, 1.72]) and of more frequent clinical use (aOR = 2.05, 95% CI [1.75, 2.40]), with parallel associations for organizational support (aOR = 1.43 and 1.60). Nurses who were untrained and uninterested in training had markedly lower odds of both behaviours than trained nurses (aOR = 0.16 and 0.24); this comparison combines training receipt and interest and is not an estimate of training effectiveness. Uncertainty about whether a workplace policy existed, rather than its absence, was associated with lower use (aOR = 0.62 and 0.65). No statistically significant independent associations were detected for education, experience, age, gender, setting, or region, although role was associated with use. CONCLUSION: In this US-wide nonprobability sample, generative AI use was common and associated with visible workplace governance conditions and professional role. The cross-sectional design supports correlational, not causal, conclusions. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: Communicated policy, accessible training, and frontline supervisory support warrant evaluation as potential governance approaches; this study does not establish whether frequent use was safe, appropriate, or outcome-improving. IMPACT: The study addressed the lack of national evidence linking workplace governance to nurses' reported use of generative AI. Use was common and associated with supervisor support, training status (receipt and interest among untrained respondents), policy awareness, and professional role. The findings will inform nurses, nurse managers, health system leaders, and policy bodies responsible for evaluating and governing these tools. REPORTING METHOD: Reporting followed the STROBE guidelines for cross-sectional studies. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: No Patient or Public Contribution. This survey of practicing nurses did not involve patients or members of the public in its design, conduct, analysis, or the preparation of the manuscript.

papers.title: Meditation attenuates the ownership-identification link: a mechanism for decentering in self-referential processing.
papers.abstract: Mindfulness and acceptance-based approaches propose that psychological suffering is maintained by cognitive fusion, in which individuals become entangled with the content of their private events. The present research examined psychological ownership as a contextual mechanism linking emotional valuation to self-referential responding and tested whether brief mindfulness practice alters this functional relation. Across two studies, we investigated whether emotionally salient experiences are more likely to be experienced as "mine," thereby increasing identification with mental events, and whether mindfulness disrupts this process without reducing emotional valuation. papers.title: Interplay of mindfulness, self-compassion and mental health among young Iranian university students: mediating role of cognitive emotion regulation.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: During the pivotal college years, mental health emerges as a paramount concern, with implications for academic success, personal growth and overall well-being. AIMS: To investigate the dynamics of mindfulness and self-compassion, exploring their roles in enhancing the mental well-being of 246 young Iranian adults in full-time university study during the academic year of 2022-2023. METHOD: Utilising standardised questionnaires and structural equation modelling, we examined the relationships between participants' mindfulness, self-compassion and cognitive emotion regulation and their mental health. RESULTS: Mindfulness, self-compassion and adaptive cognitive emotion regulation showed positive correlations with mental health. Adaptive cognitive emotion regulation emerged as a key mediator in the relationship between self-compassion and mental health ( CONCLUSIONS: Interventions aimed at enhancing mindfulness, self-compassion and adaptive cognitive emotion regulation hold promise in improving the mental health of young adults in full-time study.

papers.title: MBCT improves working memory and sustained attention in generalized anxiety disorder: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) is a promising intervention for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Although GAD is associated with cognitive impairments, it remains unclear whether MBCT benefits cognitive functioning in clinical practice. This study examined outcomes of MBCT among adults with GAD in a routine clinical setting. METHODS: In this assessor blinded randomized trial, 140 adults with GAD received 8 weeks of group-based MBCT or structured psychoeducation alongside stable pharmacological treatment. Anxiety, mindfulness, working memory, sustained attention, and inhibitory control were assessed at baseline and post-intervention. Linear mixed models tested intervention effects, and within-group regression analyses examined factors associated with cognitive improvement. RESULTS: GAD patients receiving MBCT showed greater reductions in clinician-rated and self-reported anxiety and greater improvements in mindfulness, sustained attention, and working memory than those receiving psychoeducation. No between group difference in change was found for inhibitory control. Within the MBCT group, lower baseline cognitive performance predicted greater gains. Reduced self-reported anxiety was associated with working memory and subsequent sustained attention gains. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the effectiveness of MBCT in reducing anxiety symptoms and increasing mindfulness in adults with GAD. MBCT also improved sustained attention and working memory without significantly affecting inhibitory control. Cognitive gains varied with baseline performance, self-reported anxiety reduction, and improvement in related cognitive domains. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2400090284.

papers.title: Differential effects of focused attention and open monitoring meditation on varied prospective memory tasks.
papers.abstract: Mindfulness meditation can help individuals consciously maintain their attention on present stimuli. This form of mental training incorporates both focused attention (FA) and open monitoring (OM) techniques. These distinct methods cultivate separate cognitive skills related to awareness, suggesting their impact on various categories of prospective remembering could differ significantly. This study recruited 108 participants and adopted a 4 (groups: FA group, OM group, control group, baseline group) × 3 (types: high-overlap, low-overlap, dual-stimuli) mixed experimental design to investigate whether FA and OM have different effects on different types of prospective memory. The results showed that FA primarily enhanced prospective memory performance under the low-overlap condition, whereas OM significantly facilitated prospective memory under both high-overlap and dual-stimuli conditions. The results indicated that there are variations in the enhancement of prospective memory between FA and OM. FA meditation primarily facilitates prospective memory under conditions of low processing overlap, whereas OM meditation shows stronger benefits in contexts characterized by high processing overlap and increased stimulus complexity.
